'''''Oenanthe crocata''''', '''hemlock water-dropwort''' (sometimes known as '''dead man's fingers''') is a [[flowering plant]] in the [[Apiaceae|carrot family]], native to [[Europe]], [[North Africa]] and western [[Asia]]. It grows in damp grassland and wet woodland, often along river and stream banks. All parts of the plant are extremely toxic and it has been known to cause human and livestock poisoning.

==Description==
Hemlock water-dropwort is a robust hairless [[perennial]] growing up to 150 cm tall with hollow, cylindrical, grooved stems up to {{convert|3.5|cm}} across. The stems are often branched. The upper part of the roots include five or more obovoid, pale yellow, fleshy tubers up to {{convert|6|cm}} long, which exude a yellowish oily fluid when cut that stains the skin.<ref name=Tutin>{{cite book |last1=Tutin |first1=T.G. |title=Umbellifers of the British Isles |date=1980 |publisher=Botanical Society of the British Isles |location=London}}</ref>

[[File:Oenanthe crocata leaflets.jpg|thumb|Foliage of hemlock water-dropwort]]
The lower leaves are 3–4 times [[pinnate]], triangular, with oval toothed leaflets {{convert|10-20|mm}} long, that are basally tapered to the stalk ([[Glossary_of_leaf_morphology#cuneate|cuneate]]). The upper leaves are 1–2 pinnate, with narrower lobes and a shorter [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] (leaf stalk). All the leaves are spirally arranged and have petioles that are slightly sheathing around the stem. The leaves have a characteristically deceptive odour of [[parsley]] or [[celery]].<ref name=Rose>{{cite book |last1=Rose |first1=Francis |title=The Wild Flower Key |date=2006 |publisher=Frederick Warne |location=London|isbn=978-0-7232-5175-0}}</ref><ref name = "Newman">Newman J. 2005. CEH Information Sheet 31: ''Oenanthe crocata'' (Hemlock Water-Dropwort).</ref>

Like other species in the genus, hemlock water-dropwort has compound [[umbel]]s, with 12–40 smooth rays (stalks), {{convert|3-8|cm}} aclong, which carry the smaller umbellules. These rays are shorter than the stalk ([[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]]) below, and they do not become thicker after flowering. At the base of the rays are about five [[bract]]s, which are linear to trifid in shape. These umbels are either terminal (at the top of the stem) or lateral (in the leaf axils).
[[File:Oenanthe crocata flowers.jpg|thumb|Close-up of the flowers]]
[[File:Oenanthe crocata fruiting umbel.jpg|thumb|Fruits of hemlock water-dropwort]]

The umbellules, which are {{convert|5-10|cm}} in diameter, have 6 or more bracteoles at their base and numerous flowers on short [[pedicel (botany)|pedicels]]. The flowers are white, almost [[actinomorphic]] with five subequal petals, the outer ones being slightly larger. There are also five conspicuous [[sepal]]s which are triangular, sharply pointed, and persistent. The terminal umbels have mostly bisexual flowers; the lateral ones have mostly male flowers. The flowers have five [[stamen]]s and (if present) two [[style (botany)|styles]], with an enlarged base forming a structure called a stylopodium. The cylindrical fruits are {{convert|4-6|mm}} ac long, with styles measuring {{convert|2|mm}} in length.<ref name="Tutin" /><ref name=Sell3>{{cite book |last1=Sell |first1=Peter |last2=Murrell |first2=Gina |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland, vol 3 |date=2009 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}}</ref>

This species usually flowers in June and July in northern Europe.<ref>Gibbons B. & Brough, P. 2008. ''Guide to Wildflowers of Britain and Northern Europe''. Philips</ref>

==Identification==
[[File:Oenanthe crocata rays and bracts.jpg|thumb|Rays and bracts of a primary umbel]]
Hemlock water-dropwort is easily separated from the other water-dropworts in Britain by its greater size, its broad, flat leaflets, and the long, thin bracts on the primary umbels. It is more likely to be confused with species in other genera, including perhaps [[Cicuta virosa|cowbane]] or [[Sium latifolium|greater water-parsnip]]. The former has no bracts and latter has upper leaves which are just once pinnate, while hemlock water-dropwort always has at least ternate leaflets (divided into three parts).<ref name="Tutin" />

==Taxonomy and nomenclature==
[[File:Oenanthe_crocata_bracteoles.jpg|thumb|Atypically large and numerous bracteoles on an immature umbel]]
[[File:Oenanthe crocata hollow stem.jpg|thumb|Section of a cut stem, which had a diameter of 3.2 cm]]
Although hemlock water-dropwort has been recognised as a distinct plant for centuries, the modern definition was worked out by [[Peter Artedi|Artedius]] in the early 18th century, and the name was published by [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] in 1753 in ''[[Species Plantarum]]''.<ref name=constance>{{cite book |last1=Constance |first1=L. |title=History of the classification of Umbelliferae (Apiaceae) ''in Heywood, V. H. (ed.) The Biology and Chemistry of the Umbelliferae''|date=1971 |publisher=Academic Press |location=London |pages=1–11}}</ref>

It has several synonyms (i.e. other authors have named the same plant, but the Linnaean name for it stands), including ''O. apiifolia'' Brot. (1804), ''Phellandrium plinii'' Bubani (1899), ''Oenanthe macrosciadia'' Willk. (1852) and ''O. gallaecica'' Pau & Merino (1904). A full list can be found in the Synonymic Checklists of the Plants of the World.<ref name=gbif602/><ref>{{cite web |last1=Hassler |first1=M. |title=Synonymic Checklists of the Vascular Plants of the World |date=2024 |publisher=ChecklistBank |doi=10.48580/dgjc7-3dd |url=https://www.gbif.org/dataset/be1f0e7a-0ee0-45a8-847c-9d12e3997425}}</ref>

It has no [[subspecies]], but numerous [[Variety (botany) | varieties]] have been named, none of which is in common use today.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Global Biodiversity Information Facility |title=Oenanthe crocata L. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/6027319 |access-date=27 April 2022}}</ref>

There are no recorded hybrids.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=Hybridization and the Flora of the British Isles |date=1975 |publisher=Academic Press |location=London |isbn=0-12-661650-7}}</ref>

Its chromosome number is 2n = 22 (based on British specimens).<ref name="Tutin" />

The generic name ''[[Oenanthe (plant)|Oenanthe]]'', which comes from the [[Ancient Greek]] οίνος, "wine" and άνθος, "flower", was used in ancient times for certain Mediterranean plants and later adopted to describe this genus. The specific epithet "crocata" comes from the same root as crocus, and refers to the saffron-yellow colour of the oil that exudes from ducts in the tubers,<ref name="King" /> although this is difficult to observe in fresh specimens.<ref name=Stearn>{{cite book |last1=Stearn |first1=William T. |title=Botanical Latin: History, Grammar, Syntax, Terminology and Vocabulary |date=1980 |publisher=David & Charles |location=Newton Abbot |isbn=0-7153-5645-3}}</ref><ref name=Leighton>{{cite book |last1=Leighton |first1=W.A. |title=A Flora of Shropshire |date=1841 |publisher=John van Voorst |location=London}}</ref>
The common name "dropwort" refers to the drop-shaped tubers found amongst the roots of certain species in this genus.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Wiktionary |title=dropwort |date=18 August 2024 |url=https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/dropwort}}</ref> The "hemlock" part is possibly because of the plant's superficial resemblance to ''[[Conium maculatum]]''.

In older botanical works, the [[Planet symbols|planet symbol]] for Jupiter (♃) sometimes appears by the name.<ref name="Leighton" /> This is simply a code to show that the plant is a perennial.<ref name="Stearn" />

==Distribution and status==
The native distribution of hemlock water-dropwort is concentrated along the [[Atlantic]] seaboard of Europe, from the coast of the [[Netherlands]] south to [[Portugal]] and [[Spain]], rapidly becoming rare inland. It is common again in [[Corsica]] and [[Sardinia]] but otherwise only sparsely distributed around the [[Mediterranean]] east to [[Syria]] and southwards to [[Morocco]]. It is perhaps most common in [[Great Britain|Britain]] and [[Ireland]], where it is widespread throughout, even in inland locations.<ref>Streeter D, Hart-Davis C, Hardcastle A, Cole F, Harper L. 2009. ''Collins Wildflower Guide''. HarperCollins.</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Global Biodiversity Information Facility |title=Oenanthe crocata L. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/6027319 |access-date=2 May 2022}}</ref>

There are few records of it as an introduction outside its native range, although it has been reported from Argentina.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Martínez |first1=S. |last2=Calviño |first2=C.I. |last3=Delucchi |first3=G. |title=Oenanthe crocata (Apiaceae, Apioideae), new toxic plant for adventitious flora of Argentina and America |journal=Darwiniana |date=2012 |volume=50 |issue=1 |pages=97–106 |url=https://www.cabdirect.org/cabdirect/abstract/20133214937}}</ref>

In France, where it is known as {{lang|fr|oenanthe jaune safran}}, it is considered unthreatened ("Least Concern", or LC), although in some départements it is rarer; for example, in [[Île-de-France]] and [[Picardy]] it is classified as Critically Endangered (CR).<ref>{{cite web |last1=Inventaire National du Patrimoine Naturel |title=Œnanthe jaune safran |url=https://inpn.mnhn.fr/espece/cd_nom/109864 |access-date=8 June 2022}}</ref> In Britain, it is similarly listed as LC.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cheffings |first1=C.M. | last2=Farrell |first2=L. |title=The Vascular Plant Red Data List for Great Britain |date=2005 |publisher=Joint Nature Conservation Committee |location=Peterborough}}</ref>

==Habitat and ecology==
[[File:Oenanthe crocata clump.jpg|thumb|A sprawling plant of hemlock water-dropwort in crack willow carr by the river Stour in Kent]]
Hemlock water-dropwort is a plant of shallow fresh water streams, marshes, lakes, ponds, canals and wet woodland.<ref name = "Newman"/> It is usually a [[calcifuge]], and as a lowland species it nearly always occurs below 300 m,<ref name = "Newman"/> although in Britain it is found as high as 340 m in the [[Brecon Beacons]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Pearman |first1=D.A. |title=Altitudinal Limits of British Plants, 2021 |url=https://bsbi.org/altitudes}}</ref> In Wales, where it is known as {{lang|cy|cegiden y dŵr}}, it is reported to be salt-tolerant, and is known on the inland edges of salt marshes and even on harbour walls.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Chater |first1=A.O. |title=Flora of Cardiganshire |date=2010 |publisher=A.O. Chater |location=Aberystwyth |isbn=9-780956-575005}}</ref>
[[File:Oenanthe crocata sward at Marden.jpg|thumb|A stand of hemlock water-dropwort in yorkshire fog grassland at Marden, Kent, England]]

Although it is widespread in a variety of wetland types, there are two main habitats for this species: woodland and grassland. In woodland, it is found in alder [[carr (landform)|carr]] (mainly [[British NVC community W5|W5 ''Alnus glutinosa'']] in Britain) in bogs and peaty river valleys, and willow carr (chiefly W6 ''[[Salix x fragilis]]'') in river [[floodplain]]s. In both these communities, it can become abundant in open areas where the trees have been thinned by flooding. In alder carr in particular, it is sometimes found with [[Cicuta virosa|cowbane]], which it strongly resembles.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Rodwell |first1=J.S. |title=British Plant Communities, vol. 1: woodlands and scrub |year=1991 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}}</ref><ref name=Lockton>{{cite book |last1=Lockton |first1=Alex |last2=Whild |first2=Sarah |title=The Flora and Vegetation of Shropshire |date=2015 |publisher=Shropshire Botanical Society |location=Montford Bridge |url=https://archive.org/details/flora-and-vegetation-of-shropshire-2015}}</ref>

In grassland, the main habitat is MG10 [[Holcus lanatus|yorkshire fog]] grassland, which is typically a kind of rush-pasture with associates such as [[Iris pseudacorus|yellow flag]], [[Juncus effusus|soft rush]] and [[Cardamine pratensis|cuckooflower]]. It is common throughout the British lowlands, extending into the upland fringes. It is most abundant in such a habitat, sometimes forming dense stands alongside ditches or around pools and extending over hundreds of square metres.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Rodwell |first1=J.S. |title=British Plant Communities, vol. 3: grasslands and montane communities|year=1992 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}}</ref><ref name="Lockton" />
[[File:Oenanthe crocata with Dilophus cf febrilis.jpg|thumb|An umbel with numerous St Mark's flies, ''Dilophus'' cf. ''febrilis'']]

Its [[Indicator value|Ellenberg values]] in Britain are L = 7, F = 8, R = 6, N = 7, and S = 1, which show that it favours damp, reasonably sunny places with neutral soils and moderate fertility, and that it can occur in slightly brackish situations.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hill|first1=M.O.|last2=Mountford|first2=J.O.|last3=Roy|first3=D.B.|last4=Bunce|first4=R.G.H.|title=Ellenberg's indicator values for British plants. ECOFACT Volume 2. Technical Annex|date=1999|publisher=Institute of Terrestrial Ecology|isbn=1870393481|url=http://nora.nerc.ac.uk/6411/1/ECOFACT2a.pdf|accessdate=29 May 2017}}</ref>

The flowers are unspecialised, meaning they can be pollinated by many species of insect, which are attracted to the nectar that is secreted onto the exposed surface of the stylopodium.<ref name="Tutin" />

[[File:Depressaria_daucella_with_Oenanthe_crocata.jpg|thumb|Larva of ''Depressaria daucella'' on a defoliated plant of hemlock water-dropwort]]
Despite its toxicity, there are several species of insect which feed on hemlock water-dropwort. In Britain, these include three types of beetle: ''[[Prasocuris phellandrii]]'', ''Hypera adspersa'' and ''Hypera pollux''; and three species of fly: ''[[Elachiptera cornuta]]'', ''[[carrot fly|Chamaepsila rosae]]'' and ''[[Cheilosia impressa]]''. There is also one [[hemiptera|bug]], ''Cavariella aegopodii'', and three types of [[Lepidoptera]] (micro-moths): ''[[Depressaria daucella]]'', ''[[Depressaria ultimella|D. ultimella]]'' and ''[[Agonopterix yeatiana]]''.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Biological Records Centre |title=Insects and their food plants |url=https://www.brc.ac.uk/dbif/hostsresults.aspx?hostid=3622 |access-date=22 May 2022 }}{{Dead link|date=December 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> The larvae of the fly ''[[Euleia heraclei]]'' also mine the leaves of this species.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Pitkin |first1=B. |title=Euleia heraclei (Linnaeus, 1758) |url=http://www.ukflymines.co.uk/Flies/Euleia_heraclei.php |website=The leaf and stem mines of British flies and other insects |access-date=9 November 2022}}</ref>

==Toxicity==
The toxic principle in the plant is [[oenanthotoxin]], a polyunsaturated fatty alcohol that works by blocking [[γ-aminobutyric acid]] (GABA) receptors. The plant is very poisonous to humans and livestock and can cause death if poisoning is left untreated after ingestion. Symptoms in livestock include increased salivation, dilated pupils, respiratory distress, and convulsions. Cattle poisoning from this plant occurs sporadically. For example, several cases were reported during the [[1995 British Isles heat wave|1995 drought]] in the [[West Country]], England. Due to the shortage of grass in the fields, the cattle were driven to graze by ditches where hemlock water-dropwort grew.<ref name = "Mabey">Mabey R. 1996. ''Flora Britannica''. Random House.</ref>

Instances of poisoning in humans are rare, with only 13 cases reported in Britain between 1900 and 1978, mostly involving children. However, 9 of these 13 were fatal.<ref name=King>{{cite journal |last1=King |first1=L.A. |last2=Lewis |first2=M.J. |last3=Parry |first3=D. | last4= Twitchett |first4=P.J.|last5=Kilner |first5=E.A. |title=Identification of Oenanthotoxin and Related Compounds in Hemlock Water Dropwort Poisoning |journal=Human Toxicology |date=1985 |volume=4 |issue=4 |pages=355–364 |doi=10.1177/096032718500400401|pmid=4018815 }}</ref> Serious cases usually involved consumption of the roots, which were mistaken for [[parsnip]].<ref name = "Mabey"/><ref name = "Downs">Downs C., Philips J., Ranger G., Farrel L. 2002. [https://emj.bmj.com/content/19/5/472.long A hemlock water-dropwort curry: a case of multiple poisoning.] ''Emergency Medical Journal'' 19: 472 – 473</ref> Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, seizures, hallucinations, [[ataxia]], and haemorrhaging of the brain and lungs.<ref name = "Ball">Ball M.J., Flather M.L., Forfar J.C. 1987. Hemlock water dropwort poisoning. ''Postgraduate Medical Journal'' 63: 363 – 365.</ref> Accidental splashing of some sap in the eye of a laboratory worker led to symptoms of poisoning that lasted 12 hours.<ref name=poison>{{cite book |last1=Cooper |first1=M.R. |last2=Johnson |first2=A.W. |last3=Dauncey |first3=E.A. |title=Poisonous Plants and Fungi |date=2003 |publisher=The Stationery Office |location=London |isbn=0-11-702861-4}}</ref> The Scottish botanist [[John Lightfoot (biologist)|John Lightfoot]], in his 'Flora Scotica' (1777) related the experience of the illustrator Georg Ehret, who found that "the smell, or effluvia only, rendered him so giddy that he was several times obliged to quit the room" until he opened the door and windows so that he could finish his work.<ref>Flora Scotica. By the Revd John Lightfoot. Volume 1. London MDCCLXXVII (1777). Page 162. https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/62654#page/222/mode/1up</ref> Being a [[polyyne]], oenanthotoxin is quite unstable, and boiling the roots both lessens the severity of the symptoms and prolongs the delay before they appear.<ref name = "Downs"/>

==Uses and in culture==
Scientists at the [[University of Eastern Piedmont]] in Italy wrote that they had identified ''Oenanthe crocata'' as the plant responsible for producing the [[Risus sardonicus|sardonic grin]].<ref>[http://www.scientificamerican.com/article.cfm?id=in-brief-aug-09 News Scan Briefs: Killer Smile], ''Scientific American'', August 2009</ref><ref name=app>{{cite journal|journal = Journal of Natural Products|year = 2009|volume = 72|issue = 5|pages = 962–965|title = Polyacetylenes from Sardinian ''Oenanthe fistulosa'': A Molecular Clue to ''risus sardonicus''|author1=G. Appendino |author2=F. Pollastro |author3=L. Verotta |author4=M. Ballero |author5=A. Romano |author6=P. Wyrembek |author7=K. Szczuraszek |author8=J. W. Mozrzymas |author9=O. Taglialatela-Scafati |name-list-style=amp |doi = 10.1021/np8007717|pmid = 19245244|pmc = 2685611}}</ref> The poison constricts the muscles causing death by asphyxia which causes a death grin, the sardonic grin.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.wildfooduk.com/wild-plants/hemlock-water-dropwort|title=WildFoodUK: Hedgerow Guide - Hemlock Water Dropwort|accessdate=29 June 2025}}</ref> This plant is a possible candidate for the "sardonic herb", which was  a [[Neurotoxin|neurotoxic]] plant referred to in ancient histories. It was purportedly used for the [[Human sacrifice|ritual killing]] of elderly people and criminals in [[Nuragic civilization|Nuragic]] [[Sardinia]]. The subjects were [[Substance intoxication|intoxicated]] with the herb and then dropped from a high rock or beaten to death.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Appendino|first1=Giovanni|last2=Pollastro|first2=Federica|last3=Verotta|first3=Luisella|last4=Ballero|first4=Mauro|last5=Romano|first5=Adriana|last6=Wyrembek|first6=Paulina|last7=Szczuraszek|first7=Katarzyna|last8=Mozrzymas|first8=Jerzy W.|last9=Taglialatela-Scafati|first9=Orazio|date=2009-05-22|title=Polyacetylenes from Sardinian Oenanthe fistulosa: A Molecular Clue to risus sardonicus|journal=Journal of Natural Products|volume=72|issue=5|pages=962–965|doi=10.1021/np8007717|issn=0163-3864|pmc=2685611|pmid=19245244}}</ref>

The essential oils from the seeds of ''O. crocata'' have been shown to have moderate antibacterial effect against ''[[Enterococcus faecalis]]'' and ''[[Bacillus lentus]]''.<ref>Bonsignore L, Casu L, Loy G, Deidda D, Genco F. 2004. Analysis of the essential oil of ''Oenanthe crocata'' L. and its biological activity. ''Journal of Essential Oil Research'', 16(3): 266-269.</ref> The oils are also anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and anti-fungal (esp. against ''[[Cryptococcus neoformans]]''), and they have been suggested for use in counteracting inflammatory diseases.<ref>Valente J, Zuzarte M, Gonçalves MJ, Lopes MC. Cavaleiro C, Salgueiro L, Cruz MT. 2013. Antifungal, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory activities of Oenanthe crocata L. essential oil. ''Food and chemical toxicology'' 62: 349-354.</ref> In the past, extracts from this plant have been used in medicine, for example as a treatment for epilepsy,<ref name=French>{{cite book | author=French, D.H. | chapter= Ethnobotany of the Umbelliferae | editor=Heywood, V.H.| title=The Biology and Chemistry of the Umbelliferae | publisher=Academic Press | date=1971 | pages=385–412 | isbn=0-12-346940-6}}</ref> and in [[Ireland]] it was apparently commonly used in a poultice for treating skin disorders and even cancers.<ref name=Allen>{{Cite book |last1=Allen |first1=D.E. |url=https://archive.org/details/medicinalplantsi00davi |title=Medicinal Plants in Folk Tradition |last2=Hatfield |first2=G. |year=2004 |publisher=Timber Press |isbn=0-88192-638-8}}</ref>
